chapter: Banjo career, Armstrong and the Liberty Bell
title: Tranchina's demand that Vincent read banjo parts, and the five-flat piece
summary: Vincent tells how Tranchina took over the banjo to show him up and fired a band. He was brought in with Louis Dumaine, read the music in five flats without a mistake, and won Tranchina's praise.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Okay, go ahead. Ask them about the tranchina.

Oh, the tranchina. Yeah, after they played there a while, the tranchina, they kept on, so they turned to the boys and they said, Dad can't play no banjo like this, Dad can't play no banjo like that. And, um, always banging on the set. So, at the time, they got rid of the band. They told tranchina, say, my boy, what do you call yourself doing? I said, what, Mr. Tarnes? He said, play on that banjo you got there. He said, I can play, Mr. Tarnes. He said, you can't play nothing. He said, give me that banjo. And tranchina, take that banjo man and play the devil out of it. And he was so scared we didn't know what to do. They fired the band that night. And then they got, uh, uh, uh, Celestine sent, uh, Louis to Maine there. I was playing with Louis to Maine. So Louis said, Dad, he said, I'm gonna take you out of the tranchina's house. So you heard about John there. He said, now I want you to read that music. And he said, we want to make a hit. But he said tranchina's kind of hard on the banjo. He said, you can play yourself. That made me kind of scared, you know. I got all that man or a girl like that, you know. He said, Louis, you know Louis, play strict music. And then I put my music down, I said, put the music. And Louis called, you know, the numbers left behind my neck. So I said he come and did me the same thing. Turn the tie on, cross it, and sit down. That's it. And it was funny. He didn't say nothing. He just got to walk away. So Louis and I, she said, well done. He said, baby, got the job. He said, oh baby, got the job. He said, oh man, didn't say nothing. But the next night, we went out there. He listened again. The next night, he didn't say nothing. The next night, he said, let me see your banjo. He said, oh, you got it. And I played that piece, what's the call? Starters. Starters, play that. And I don't make one mistake in it, because it's in five flats, you know. And he said, he said, my little man said he really played that he got the right compliment. So they told him to play, then he complimented. He complimented just like I did. And he told me, he said, oh, your card is perfect. That's all he told me. We said that to the clothes. We said that to the clothes.
